definition: Contextual Query Language (CQL), previously known as Common Query Language, is a formal language for representing queries to information retrieval systems such as search engines, bibliographic catalogs and museum collection information.
details: Based on the semantics of Z39.50, its design objective is that queries be human readable and writable, and that the language be intuitive while maintaining the expressiveness of more complex query languages. It is being developed and maintained by the Z39.50 Maintenance Agency, part of the Library of Congress.

explainer.lead: Contextual Query Language (CQL) is a way to write precise searches that people can still read and edit. It brings semantics based on Z39.50 to queries for search engines, bibliographic catalogs, and museum collection systems, while aiming to retain the expressiveness of more complex query languages.

tiers.eli5: Imagine writing a clear note to a librarian explaining exactly what you want to find. CQL is like a set of rules for writing that note so both a person and a search system can understand it. It tries to keep the instructions simple without losing the ability to ask detailed questions.
tiers.practitioner: Use CQL when an information retrieval interface needs formal queries that people can read and write. It applies to settings such as search engines, bibliographic catalogs, and museum collection information, with semantics based on Z39.50. Its readability does not make queries free text: conditions still need to be expressed precisely, and implementations must preserve the intended query semantics.
tiers.paperLevel: CQL is a formal language for representing a query q to an information retrieval system, with semantics based on Z39.50. Its design objective is that q be human readable and writable and intuitive, while maintaining the expressiveness of more complex query languages. CQL, previously called Common Query Language, is developed and maintained by the Z39.50 Maintenance Agency, part of the Library of Congress.

explainer.example: A museum visitor wants collection records for objects titled “Sunflowers.” That request is written as a formal CQL title query, which the collection information system interprets to find the matching records.

usedIn.name: Search engines
usedIn.detail: CQL can formally represent queries submitted to information retrieval systems.

usedIn.name: Bibliographic catalogs
usedIn.detail: It provides a human-readable way to express precise searches for catalog records.

usedIn.name: Museum collection information
usedIn.detail: It can represent queries sent to systems that provide information about museum collections.

explainer.intuition: CQL aims to make a precise query look like something a person can reasonably read and write, rather than forcing a choice between simplicity and expressive power.
howItWorks: Start with the information you want to retrieve.
Express the search conditions formally in CQL.
Give the query to an information retrieval system.
The system interprets it using semantics based on Z39.50.
The system searches the target collection and returns matching information.
explainer.whyItMatters: CQL seeks to combine precise, expressive retrieval with queries that people can understand and create themselves. Its development and maintenance by the Z39.50 Maintenance Agency connect it directly to the established Z39.50 retrieval tradition.
misconceptions: Human-readable CQL queries are still formal queries, not unrestricted natural-language questions.
CQL is not limited to bibliographic catalogs; it also represents queries for search engines and museum collection information.

diagram.caption: CQL turns a person’s search intent into a formal query that a retrieval system can interpret.
